newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises despite sharp fall in employment.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises despite sharp fall in employment.

text.p: The dollar was jostled by surprisingly weak U.S. employment data Friday but eventually rose as stocks and bonds surged in the belief the Federal Reserve will hold off raising interest rates.
The dollar weakened initially while currency traders were divided by the report, which also showed a large jump in monthly wages.

"The market is more sensitized to inflation than it is to growth right now," said John Nelson, senior vice president at ABN-AMRO Bank. "As a result the wage number was probably more important than the non-farm payroll number."
"But if you look at U.S. stocks and U.S. bonds ... I think that will add a biddish (supportive) tone to the dollar."
After earlier declines, the dollar rose to 1.5323 German marks in late New York trading from 1.5310 marks late Thursday, and to 111.79 Japanese yen from 111.47 yen.

Interest rates fell when Treasury bond prices, which move in the opposite direction from yields, gained more than a full point after the government reported U.S. payrolls contracted 40,000 last month.

The unemployment rate also rose slightly to 5.2 percent in September, from 5.1 percent in August, diminishing the odds the Fed would chose to raise interest rates when its policy makers next meet on Nov. 13.
The Dow Jones industrial average surged 60.01 points to a record high of 5,992.86 on Friday.
The dollar has rallied for most of 1996 as investors loaded up on U.S. financial instruments, believing a strong U.S. economy would keep U.S. interest rates relatively high.

With interest rates across Europe falling and yields in Japan at record-low levels, foreigners may increasingly ignore U.S. economic data. Their appetite for dollar-denominated assets should continue to fuel the dollar's rise even if yields on U.S. securities bonds did fall Friday, traders said.

"Lower interest rates are a product of assets improving in value not a lack of economic activity," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale. "It's more of a product of supply and demand for U.S. assets."

Even the Fed's surprise decision to keep short-term interest rates steady at its last meeting in September failed to derail the dollar's rally, which hit a 2-1/2-year high against the yen and a three-month high vs. the mark this week.
The jobs data seemed to validate the Fed's decision and opened up the possibility that interest rates would remain stable or even fall if the economy showed further signs of slowing.
"No matter what the numbers were it doesn't really change the market sentiment," said Dorit Ronnen, foreign exchange trader at Bank Leumi Trust Co.

"Typically, when you see a number like that they say: 'Okay the Fed is going to ease,' and the dollar would come off, but it didn't. The bond and stock markets are well bid and the dollar followed that," she added.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2579 Swiss francs from 1.2557 late Thursday. It fell to Canadian $1.3544 from C$1.3603.
The British pound eased to $1.5649 from $1.5655.
